days.title: The Hardest Decisions Hold More Than One Truth
days.text:
School leaders: A, B, C or D? ⚖️

A student admits to plagiarism. She has been caring for a sick sibling and missing support windows.

A. Full academic penalty, right away.
B. Hold accountability, and pair it with a recovery plan.
C. Delay until a counselor and teacher conference.
D. Have the grade-level team design the response.

Comment your letter. 👇

This is one of the dilemmas in Gray Area Leadership, a free module in my H.E.L.P. course for school leaders. The hardest decisions hold more than one truth at once. Link in bio.

days.label: What would you do? Scenario 05, Permission to say "shut up" (carousel; video on YouTube)
days.title: Principals: What Would You Do? Permission to Say "Shut Up"
days.text:
Principals and teachers: what would you do? 🤔

A parent sends a note. Her daughter has permission to tell another student to "shut up" if he verbally bullies her.

It's the first time the school has heard that she may be dealing with ongoing verbal bullying.

How do you teach her to stand up for herself without teaching her to become the next bully? Comment your first move. What I chose is in the first comment.

This is one of 12 real scenarios in my What Would You Do? 12 School Leadership Scenarios deck, where you make the call before you see how I handled it. Link in bio.

#principallife #schoolleadership #assistantprincipal #whatwouldyoudo #antibullying #teachertok
days.first_comment:
What I chose: I contacted the parent immediately and opened a full bullying investigation, including student interviews. Then we talked with her: it's okay to stand up for yourself, as long as you don't become a bully, and it's important to tell an adult so we can act quickly. I praised her for telling her parent.

I also told her about my own father, a principal, whose old-school advice was to punch back or shout back. I don't agree with fighting, but his larger lesson stayed with me: defending yourself properly is never wrong.

Teach children to be strong enough to speak and wise enough to seek help.

linkedin.text:
I once had a teacher candidate show up 15 minutes late for an interview.

He knew it had killed his chance of landing the job. So he walked in and said:

"Well, I know I'm not going to get the job, but I'd love to hear your interview questions for practice."

I thought that was a great way to turn a negative into a positive.

But let's be clear about the lesson. Arrive late for an interview and you've already soured the interviewer. Plan on arriving at least 30 minutes early. It gives you a cushion for any travel problems, and it looks great in the eyes of the interviewer. And if the interviewer is running ahead of schedule, you might get in early.

Principals: what's the best recovery you've ever seen from a candidate who started off on the wrong foot?

#TeacherInterview #Education #Hiring #K12

linkedin.text:
The toughest interview I ever had was a setup.

I was interviewing for a music job and was fairly confident going in. Then the interviewer pulled out my college transcripts and began challenging me on a poor grade I had received in one of my classes.

"How could you possibly consider teaching children if you couldn't earn a higher grade in your music course?"

He grilled me for several minutes. I stammered my way through an answer.

Only afterward did he tell me that my dad, a fellow educator and his friend, had told him to give me a hard time. The job was already earmarked for somebody else.

It gave me great practice for dealing with hard questions in interviews.

To every candidate heading into interview season: practice the hard questions out loud, with colleagues or friends, before the real one.

Teachers' kids: did your parent ever set you up like this?

poll.question: A student admits to plagiarism while caring for a sick sibling. What's your first move?

linkedin.text:
The hardest decisions hold more than one truth at once.

A student admits to plagiarism. She has been caring for a sick sibling and missing support windows.

Under pressure, a decision like this collapses into a false binary: consistency or compassion. Pick a side.

The leadership move is to hold both truths long enough to make a decision that is principled, humane, and defensible. Then explain the tradeoffs: "There are real tradeoffs, and here is why we chose this path."

School leaders: what's your first move?

linkedin.cta: Books (From City Streets to The Classroom)
linkedin.text:
In my book From City Streets to The Classroom, I follow one seventh grader, Adam, through a single school day.

By second period, his day has already gone wrong at home and in class.

And here's the startling fact: we are in the second period of the day, and not one adult has bothered to ask Adam what is wrong.

Every adult he passed had a chance to break the chain of events. None of them did.

A principal, or any supportive adult, could have talked to him about his concerns. An advisor program would give every child a trusted adult in the building they can go to at any time.

A child should know that there is always someone he can count on.

Principals and teachers: who is that person for the kids in your building?

#UrbanEducation #SchoolLeadership #StudentsFirst #Education
